newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dlr ends weaker, intervention test expected.
newsitem.headline: Canada dlr ends weaker, intervention test expected.

text.p: * Canada's dollar ended weaker on Thursday at C$1.4005 (US$0.7140) from this morning's open around C$1.3985 (US$0.7150) in moderate trade, dealers said.
* They said the currency came under renewed pressure from short sellers in afternoon trade, pushing the unit toward levels where the Bank of England intervened overnight.

"I think they (corporate investors) want to find out where the central banks are going to be in again," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange advisor at CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc. "I think there is just a certain curiosity and I assume they will be in between C$1.4015 (US$0.7135) and C$1.4020 (US$0.7132)."

London foreign exchange traders told Reuters earlier that the overnight slide of the Canada dollar propelled the Bank of England to intervene and buy Canada dollars on behalf of the Bank of Canada in support of the currency between C$1.4005 and C$1.4018 early today during European trading hours.

Analysts said that merchandise trade numbers released today by Statistics Canada did little to prop up the dollar. The government reported that Canada's February trade surplus rose to C$2.19 billion. A Reuters forecast predicted the trade surplus would jump C$2.35 billion.

"It's a wet noodle for the currency," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed income analyst with MMS International. "The numbers are a tad supportive, but they could have been much better. A number like C$3 billion would have been much more convincing."

The Canadian dollar has come under increasing pressure since the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its interest rate targets and forced spreads of Canadian short-term interest rates to widen to about 250 basis below U.S rates.
Traders said the higher U.S. rates caused a selloff in Canadian short-term debt over the past month as international investors headed for the higher premiums.
The Canadian dollar has weakened because of the selloff and the Bank of Canada's refusal to raise its own rates in tandem with those in the United States.
Canada's economy has shown little sign of enough inflationary pressure to warrant a rise in interest rates.
Unemployment is high at 9.3 percent and many economists estimated the output gap or the difference between Canada's potential output and its actual productivity was about three to five percent.
Economists said Canada's recovery could be threatened if the Bank of Canada raised rates.
On the crosses, Canada's dollar fell to 1.2314 marks from Wednesday's close of 1.2364 marks, but firmed to 89.93 yen from 89.87 yen.
((Paul Casciato, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100 or email: paul.casciato@reuters.com))
